questions.q: State the audible range of the human ear.
questions.a: The human audible range is approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds within this range can be detected by the human ear. A wrong answer (e.g., "0 to infinity") ignores the physical limits of the ear — there are specific lower and upper bounds.

questions.q: Define infrasound and ultrasound with their frequency ranges.
questions.a: Infrasound: sound with frequency below 20 Hz — inaudible to humans, often felt as vibration (e.g., earthquakes, elephant communication). Ultrasound: sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz — inaudible to humans, used in medical imaging, industrial cleaning, and animal echolocation (bats, dolphins). A wrong answer (e.g., "infrasound is low volume") confuses frequency with amplitude — infrasound is low frequency, not low volume.

questions.q: Why does the upper limit of hearing decrease with age?
questions.a: The hair cells in the inner ear that detect high frequencies are more fragile and degrade with age. As these cells are lost, the ability to hear high frequencies decreases. A young person might hear up to 20,000 Hz, while a 60-year-old might only hear up to 12,000 Hz. This is called presbycusis (age-related hearing loss). A wrong answer (e.g., "the ear gets tired") is incorrect — it is a physical degradation of hair cells, not fatigue.

questions.q: Give one example each of infrasound and ultrasound in nature or technology.
questions.a: Infrasound: Elephants communicate using infrasound (below 20 Hz) over long distances. Earthquakes produce infrasound. Ultrasound: Bats use ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz) for echolocation to navigate and hunt. Medical ultrasound imaging uses frequencies of 2-15 MHz to visualize internal organs. A wrong answer (e.g., "infrasound is used in hospitals") confuses infrasound with ultrasound — medical imaging uses ultrasound, not infrasound.

questions.q: A "mosquito ringtone" has frequency 17,000 Hz. Can a 15-year-old and a 50-year-old hear it? Explain.
questions.a: The 15-year-old can likely hear it — 17,000 Hz is within the audible range of young people (up to 20,000 Hz). The 50-year-old likely cannot — the upper limit decreases with age, and a 50-year-old might only hear up to 15,000 Hz or lower. This is why mosquito ringtones are used by students to receive phone calls without teachers hearing. A wrong answer (e.g., "both can hear it") ignores the age-related decline in high-frequency hearing.

questions.q: A student says: "If a sound is very loud, it must be within the audible range." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Loudness (amplitude) and audibility (frequency range) are independent. An infrasound wave (below 20 Hz) can be very loud (high amplitude) but still inaudible — you might feel it as vibration but not hear it. An ultrasound wave (above 20,000 Hz) can be very loud but inaudible. Loudness does not determine whether a sound is audible — frequency does. A sound must be within 20-20,000 Hz to be audible, regardless of its loudness. A wrong evaluation (agreeing with the student) confuses amplitude (loudness) with frequency (audibility).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The audible range is the range of sound frequencies that the human ear can detect: ______ 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
Fill in the blank: The lowest ______ you can hear is about 20 Hz — a deep rumble.
Fill in the blank: The lowest sound you can hear is about ______ Hz — a deep rumble.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can state the audible range (20 Hz - 20,000 Hz), define infrasound and ultrasound, explain why the upper limit decreases with age, and give examples of sounds within and outside the audible range.
